source.title: Using GANs for Sharing Networked Time Series Data: Challenges, Initial Promise, and Open Questions

accepted.question_text: For networking datasets in which each sample contains fixed metadata together with an associated multivariate time series, can generative adversarial networks be used to create synthetic datasets that remain high-fidelity and generalize across downstream networking tasks without requiring substantial human expertise about workload characteristics or target tasks?

evidence.quote: The overarching question for our work is: Can we create high-fidelity, easily generalizable synthetic datasets for networking applications that require minimal (if any) human expertise regarding workload characteristics and downstream tasks?

accepted.question_text: When releasing synthetic networked time-series data generated by GANs, what privacy definition should be used for a given data-sharing use case, given that different release scenarios may require different protection goals and threat models?

evidence.quote: A meta question, not unique to our work, is finding the right definition of privacy for each use case.

accepted.question_text: In GAN-based sharing of networked time-series datasets, can the generator support flexible notions of privacy in practice, and if so, under what training or generation configurations can those privacy notions be achieved?

evidence.quote: Natural questions arise: First, can GANs support these flexible notions of privacy in practice, and if so under what configurations?

accepted.question_text: Do privacy-preserving GAN training methods achieve a privacy-fidelity tradeoff that is practical for networking datasets, where the synthetic output must preserve realistic temporal structure and cross-feature relationships while still offering meaningful privacy guarantees?

evidence.quote: Second, there are emerging proposals to extend GAN training (e.g., [40, 112, 113]) to offer some privacy guarantees. Are their privacy-fidelity tradeoffs sufficient to be practical for networking datasets?

accepted.question_text: For networking and systems datasets that consist of time series and metadata rather than labeled images, how should GAN fidelity be evaluated when the standard, widely used GAN metrics were designed for image data and cannot be directly applied?

evidence.quote: Evaluating GAN fidelity is notoriously difficult [72, 114]; the most widely-accepted metrics are designed for labelled image data [55, 92] and cannot be applied to our datasets.

accepted.question_text: When a synthetic data generator models both per-sample attributes and associated time-series records, how can practitioners realistically tune the attribute distributions of the released synthetic dataset while still preserving the conditional behavior between those attributes and the generated records?

evidence.quote: A major open question is how to realistically tune attribute distributions.

accepted.question_text: Can GAN training for synthetic systems and networking data be combined with simulators that encode the physical constraints of the underlying system, so that data generation benefits both from statistical learning and from domain-knowledge constraints?

evidence.quote: Learning to train GANs with simulators that can model physical constraints of systems may be a good way to combine the statistical learning properties of GANs with systems that encode domain knowledge.

accepted.question_text: Can differentially private GAN mechanisms for time-series generation be improved enough to provide meaningful privacy guarantees without destroying the fidelity of the generated time-series data?

evidence.quote: Our results suggest that DP-GAN mechanisms require significant improvements for privacy-preserving time series generation.

accepted.question_text: For networked time-series datasets in which one released sample may summarize behavior of many users or entities rather than a single person, is differential privacy an appropriate privacy metric for the data-sharing problem at all?
accepted.context_brief: Is differential privacy the right metric?

evidence.quote: So it is not clear whether DP is a good metric for this class of data.

accepted.question_text: If differential privacy is not well aligned with GAN-generated networked time-series releases, what alternative privacy metrics should be explored for this form of synthetic data sharing?

evidence.quote: More broadly, we believe there is value to exploring different privacy metrics.

accepted.question_text: How can synthetic-data generation methods such as DoppelGANger be extended to handle networking datasets whose behavior depends on causal interactions between stateful agents rather than only on isolated per-agent traces?

evidence.quote: Moreover, many networking datasets require significantly more complexity than DG is currently able to handle, such as causal interactions between stateful agents.

accepted.question_text: How can practitioners perform what-if analysis by modeling changes in an underlying networking system and then generating synthetic data for the modified system, especially when larger interventions invalidate the conditional distributions learned from the original data and may therefore require explicit physical-system modeling or simulation?

evidence.quote: Another direction of interest is to enable 'what-if' analysis, in which practitioners can model changes in the underlying system and generate associated data.
Such what-if analysis is likely to require physical system modeling/simulation, while GANs may be able to help model individual agent behavior.
